promptHtml: Vivado put the product of lesson 6.3's mul16 in one DSP48E1. Below is the DSP table of its Utilization report.
explanationHtml: Read the DSPs row across to Available: 240, the DSP48E1s on this chip, whatever the design uses. mul16 uses 1 of them, so its Util% is 1 ÷ 240 × 100 = 0.42.
excerpt: |    Site Type   | Used | Fixed | Prohibited | Available | Util% |
ask: How many DSP blocks does the chip have?

promptHtml: This is lesson 6.4's Listing 1: the Slice Logic table of mul16_nodsp, the 16 by 16 multiplier built with no DSP block allowed.
explanationHtml: Read the Slice LUTs row across to Util%: 0.47. The product takes 301 of the chip's 63,400 LUTs, and 301 ÷ 63,400 × 100 = 0.47, about half of one percent. With a DSP block allowed, mul16 took no LUT at all, and one of the 240 DSP blocks.
excerpt: |        Site Type        | Used | Fixed | Prohibited | Available | Util% |
ask: What is the Util% of mul16_nodsp's Slice LUTs?

promptHtml: peek_bug is level 1's LED that should show sw while peek is 1 and be 0 while peek is 0. Vivado built it, and its Slice Logic table counts one Register as Latch, where this design should have no register at all. Pick the line that makes the latch.
explanationHtml: if (peek) led = sw; gives led no value while peek is 0, so led must keep the value it had: a latch (lesson 1.4), which the report counts among its registers. An else that sets led to 0 gives it a value on every pass through the block, and the latch goes.

lines.text: // led shows sw while peek is 1, and should be 0 while peek is 0.

promptHtml: peek_bug is level 1's LED that should show sw while peek is 1 and be 0 while peek is 0. It has no clock, so it should have no register of any kind. Below is the Slice Logic table of its Utilization report.
explanationHtml: Read the Register as Latch row: 1. Slice Registers counts it too, and Register as Flip Flop is 0. A design that should hold nothing has a latch when some block leaves a value unassigned (lesson 1.4): here led gets no value while peek is 0, so it keeps the last one.
excerpt: |        Site Type        | Used | Fixed | Prohibited | Available | Util% |
ask: How many latches does peek_bug use?

promptHtml: sum_reg_bug's code keeps a + b in a 9-bit register, total, at each rising edge, but Verilator warns that total is never used. Below is the Slice Logic table of its Utilization report.
explanationHtml: Read the Slice Registers row: 0, not 9. Nothing reads total, so it never reaches a port, and synthesis removed its flip-flops and the adder that fed them (lesson 6.1). The LUTs left are the adder that works out sum.
excerpt: |        Site Type        | Used | Fixed | Prohibited | Available | Util% |
ask: How many registers does sum_reg_bug use?

promptHtml: For mul16_nodsp, utilization_synth.rpt counts 337 Slice LUTs, marked with an asterisk, and utilization.rpt, after place and route, counts 301. Why do they differ?
explanationHtml: Between the two reports, Vivado works on the netlist again before placing it, and that merges and removes cells, as the note under the asterisk warns. Nothing is left out: a build that finishes has placed every cell its netlist needs. Both reports count LUTs the same way, and exactly.
options: The steps after synthesis tidied the netlist, merging and removing LUTs.
Placement could not fit 36 of the LUTs, so it left them out.
The two reports count LUTs in different units.
The report after synthesis rounds its counts up.
